The given condition is not an identity — it holds only for special matrices, and finding
which is the first step.
**Step 1 — expand the left side.** Matrix multiplication is **not** commutative, so the
middle terms must be kept separate:
(A + B)(A − B) = A² − AB + BA − B²
**Step 2 — compare with A² − B².** The condition says
A² − AB + BA − B² = A² − B²
so
−AB + BA = 0, that is **AB = BA**
The matrices **commute** — that is the whole content of the hypothesis.
**Step 3 — simplify ABA⁻¹.** Using AB = BA,
ABA⁻¹ = (BA)A⁻¹ = B(AA⁻¹) = B·I = **B**
**Step 4 — square it.**
(ABA⁻¹)² = B² ✓
The expression ABA⁻¹ is the **similarity transform** of B by A, and the result shows that
conjugating by a matrix that commutes with B leaves B unchanged — which is exactly what
commuting means.
Note also that (ABA⁻¹)² could be computed without the commuting property:
(ABA⁻¹)(ABA⁻¹) = AB(A⁻¹A)BA⁻¹ = AB²A⁻¹
and with AB = BA this becomes B²AA⁻¹ = B² ✓ the same answer by a slightly longer route.
The lesson is that the familiar algebraic identity (a+b)(a−b) = a² − b² **fails for
matrices** unless they commute — and the question exists to make that point.
∴ B².

| 3  2 |

**Step 4 — combine.**
value = 1 × (+1) × (−1) = **−1** ✓

The inverse of a **diagonal non-singular** matrix is again a **diagonal matrix** ✓.
**Why.** Take
A = diag(a₁, a₂, …, aₙ)
Non-singular means |A| = a₁a₂…aₙ ≠ 0, so **every** diagonal entry is non-zero. Then
**A⁻¹ = diag(1/a₁, 1/a₂, …, 1/aₙ)**
**Check it.** Multiplying two diagonal matrices multiplies the corresponding entries, so
A · A⁻¹ = diag(a₁ × 1/a₁, …, aₙ × 1/aₙ) = diag(1, 1, …, 1) = **I** ✓
So the inverse is obtained simply by **reciprocating each diagonal entry** — one of the few
cases where a matrix inverse requires no work at all.
A concrete example:
A = diag(2, 5) has A⁻¹ = diag(1/2, 1/5), and the product is the identity ✓
Why the other options fail:
**(b) scalar matrix** — a scalar matrix is diagonal with all entries **equal**. The inverse
is diagonal, but the entries are equal only if they were equal to begin with, so this is too
specific.
**(c) skew symmetric** — requires Aᵀ = −A, which forces zero diagonal entries; a diagonal
matrix with zeros on the diagonal is the zero matrix and is singular.
**(d) zero matrix** — has no inverse at all, being the most singular matrix there is.
The property generalises: the inverse of an **upper triangular** matrix is upper triangular,
and of a **lower triangular** matrix lower triangular.
∴ diagonal matrix.
